Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in HCC tumors with elevated FASN expression, a strategically optimized combination therapy employing FASN inhibitors and PPARα agonists will synergistically disrupt tumor lipid balance by concurrently limiting lipid supply and overwhelming cellular oxidative defenses. In our proposed model, FASN inhibition curtails the lipid reserves necessary for membrane synthesis, while PPARα activation pushes cancer cells into a hypermetabolic state characterized by accelerated fatty acid oxidation. This metabolic reprogramming is expected to generate ROS levels that exceed the cells’ antioxidant capacity, thereby precipitating metabolic stress and initiating apoptotic cell death across heterogeneous tumor populations, including drug-resistant cancer stem cells. Furthermore, by leveraging cutting-edge technologies—such as real-time, integrated single-cell multi-omics, metabolic flux assays, CRISPR-based screening, and AI-powered computational models—we will dynamically adjust treatment parameters to preempt compensatory mechanisms and minimize off-target effects in normal hepatocytes. This refined hypothesis integrates and builds upon the original causal reasoning while addressing critical gaps in adaptive dosage optimization and real-time monitoring of tumor metabolic states.
Abstract: In this study, we propose a precision-guided, adaptive combinatorial therapeutic strategy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) characterized by high fatty acid synthase (FASN) expression. Our approach synergistically combines FASN inhibition with PPARα agonism to disrupt tumor lipid homeostasis by depleting essential lipid reserves for membrane biosynthesis and simultaneously forcing an overactive fatty acid oxidation pathway. This dual modulation is anticipated to elevate intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) to cytotoxic levels, thereby inducing metabolic stress that triggers apoptotic cell death, including within drug-resistant cancer stem cell niches. Critically, this treatment regimen is dynamically optimized in real time using integrated single-cell multi-omics profiling, metabolic flux analysis, CRISPR-based functional screens, and AI-driven computational modeling, enabling continuous monitoring of compensatory mechanisms and precise dosage calibration. Our hypothesis builds on and refines established causal links in tumor metabolism to offer a novel, adaptive, and highly targeted therapeutic intervention in HCC.
CausalChain: HCC upregulates FASN for de novo lipogenesis -> FASN inhibition reduces lipid resources needed for membrane synthesis -> Reduced lipogenesis combined with PPARα activation enhances fatty acid oxidation -> Accelerated fatty acid oxidation elevates ROS levels and metabolic stress -> Metabolic overload triggers apoptosis
